findings.problem: TODO proposes Rayon and SmallVec for performance without any benchmark, baseline, or measurement evidence. This is folklore optimization for a fixed [u8; 4] input where Rayon parallel overhead is guaranteed to be slower than sequential iteration.
findings.failure_mode: Blindly replacing sequential .iter().map().collect() with Rayon parallel iterators on 4 elements adds thread-pool dispatch, work-sharing, and result-merging overhead that dwarfs the computation cost, producing a measurable regression.
findings.fix: Remove the TODO. If optimization is needed, return [u32, 2] or use a stack-allocated buffer. Only consider SmallVec or Rayon after benchmarking proves this is a real bottleneck, which for 4-byte inputs is highly unlikely.

findings.problem: Returns Vec<&'static str> for a fixed-size output of exactly 4 elements derived from [u8; 4]. This forces a heap allocation for data whose size is known at compile time.
findings.failure_mode: Every call to classify_four performs a heap allocation and deallocation for exactly 4 string-slice elements, increasing GC pressure and cache footprint unnecessarily.
findings.fix: Return [&'static str; 4] instead of Vec<&'static str>. This eliminates allocation entirely and makes the output size statically known.

findings.problem: No benchmark, baseline, profiler data, or allocation evidence exists for any performance claim. The TODO on line 2 makes a performance claim ('it will be faster') without workload, target hardware, input distribution, baseline number, or regression threshold.
findings.failure_mode: Per Holzman PLUS: 'No performance claim without workload, target hardware, input distribution, hot path, baseline command, baseline number, new number, variance/noise notes, and regression threshold.' Unmeasured changes risk regressing performance while adding complexity.
findings.fix: Write a benchmark comparing sequential Vec collect vs [&'static str; 4] array return. Measure latency (p50/p95/p99) and allocation count with a profiler. Only refactor if measurement proves a real bottleneck exists.

findings.problem: Uses .collect() into Vec for a fixed 4-element output. Holzman requires allocation budgets and bounded allocation discipline; hot paths should avoid per-call heap allocation.
findings.failure_mode: Each call allocates a new Vec, copies 4 usize pointers, and later deallocates. In a hot path this generates allocation traffic, cache misses, and potential allocation failure.
findings.fix: Return [&'static str; 4] directly. If the caller needs a Vec, they can collect or to_vec() from the array — pushing the allocation decision to the caller who knows whether it is needed.

findings.problem: SmallVec is proposed by folklore for a fixed 4-element output. SmallVec's stack buffer is useful when the common case is small AND the size is variable at runtime. Here the size is always exactly 4 and known at compile time.
findings.failure_mode: SmallVec<[T; N]> adds a stack buffer + heap fallback + capacity tracking overhead. For fixed-size 4, a plain array [T; 4] or Vec<[T; 4]> is strictly simpler and faster with zero runtime overhead.
findings.fix: Use [u32; 4] or [&'static str; 4] as the return type. SmallVec is only justified when the output size varies at runtime and the common case fits on the stack — neither condition holds here.

missing_evidence: no benchmark exists for the stated performance claim (Rayon/SmallVec faster)
no profiler data or allocation analysis for classify_four
no baseline measurement to compare against
no workload characterization (call frequency, input distribution, throughput requirements)
no second-ring evidence (assembly, cache-line analysis, allocation counting)
residual_risk: The function is functionally correct for its inputs but violates Holzman allocation discipline by heap-allocating per call for fixed-size output. The folklore TODO proposing Rayon/SmallVec would worsen performance for 4-element inputs. Without benchmark evidence, no optimization direction is justified. Returning [&'static str; 4] would eliminate all allocation and be measurably faster for this input size.
